7.5 Verification observability and prospective feedback diagnostic

The first completed held-out failure illustrates a limitation of confidence-led delegation: assisted Luna reported passing local checks and returned complete without consulting Sol, while the independent evaluator rejected its patch. The available journal does not retain full tool outputs, so those local test counts remain self-reported. The observation supports investigating false completion; it does not show that the model ignored a visible failing test.

A separate, unrun verification policy now asks for acceptance criteria, checks that could falsify a candidate, and material coverage gaps before completion. Its assisted variant permits seeking help for an unsupported correctness property even after a narrow check passes. Common verification guidance is matched in standalone controls. This candidate was not used in the completed held-out panel.

A prospective Aider Polyglot-derived diagnostic reserves 12 development and 24 validation tasks across six languages, excluding development exercise families from validation across languages. The maintained Aider harness provides test-error feedback for repair; this separates handling an observable failure from anticipating an unseen case. The custom conversational protocol is not an official Aider leaderboard evaluation. Visible-suite fit, automatic test-gate detection and model-initiated error recognition must be reported separately. No model trials from this diagnostic have run. The executable reservation and the prospective design retain the bounded scope and prohibit tuning on validation outcomes.

The next Pro development matrix explicitly contrasts voluntary consultation with required review, alongside matched standalone controls. Pre-consultation candidate patches and final patches will receive separate pristine-container grades after generation. This measures rescue of an observed candidate failure and distinguishes routing underuse from failure to transfer or integrate useful expert advice. A separate live context-only required-review check completed three native calls and demonstrated transfer and integration of an expert-found edge case; its six post-hoc checks are mechanism evidence, not benchmark quality or autonomous-routing performance. The larger development/validation comparison has not started model inference yet.

8 Industry-standard benchmark: a 500-task routing replay

8.1 Data and interpretation

We executed a new routing analysis on all 500 SWE-bench Verified tasks, using the ten complete public submissions dated 17 February 2026 in the official SWE-bench experiments repository (SWE-bench maintainers and submission authors 2026). Each submission uses mini-SWE-agent 2.0.0 and supplies per-instance resolution, estimated inference cost and API-call counts. This gives 5,000 recorded model–task outcomes, not 5,000 independent tasks. Costs and accuracies reconcile to every submission’s published metadata. The source revision is 40f164d5b8f1d249bf95a6df8b74b577fd8e519d; task text comes from the official task repository at 3d07b464b7b311a0cbfb5ed5b2d8a3b96f84a33d. Canonical task identifiers join the records. We did not independently establish that this later task-text snapshot is byte-identical to every original model prompt used in February.

These are new router fits and outcome replays of previously executed agents. We did not rerun those ten models, infer unseen patches, or observe their current prices. Their historical outcomes are held fixed while we select among them. This experiment measures the cost–quality opportunities and limits of pre-task selection in this portfolio. It does not identify the effect of bidirectional communication, distillation, local inference or Codex subscription consumption. Same-harness-version comparisons still differ in model-specific settings, reasoning effort, service behavior and potentially execution conditions.

The protocol and model grid were frozen before fitting. Aggregate source accuracies and prices had already been inspected during dataset selection, so this is exploratory secondary analysis, not prospective preregistration. All scripts, source hashes, folds, numerical task records and results are archived under experiments/swe-replay-001 and results/swe-replay-001.

8.2 Routing method and leakage controls

Five task folds use seed 1729. For each held-out fold, training uses only the other 400 tasks. Word unigram/bigram TF–IDF, logarithmic issue length and a repository indicator feed per-model logistic success predictors and ridge regressors of log-transformed task cost. The vectorizer and transformations are fit only on that fold’s training data. Test patches, reference solutions, trajectories, actual held-out cost and held-out outcomes are excluded from decision features. An instance identifier is used only for deterministic ties.

The primary policy allocates GPT-5.2 to half the tasks and GPT-5-mini to the remainder, ranked by predicted success gain per predicted incremental dollar. Allocation takes place within each held-out fold. A global ranking over cross-fitted predictions could otherwise let a task’s label influence competing tasks’ scores through their training folds. The within-fold quota avoids that indirect selection path. This is a batch allocation policy, not a validated online arrival-by-arrival budget controller.

Fixed single-model policies, random allocation, length and predicted-gain baselines, a declared allocation grid, and a ten-model expected-utility grid are also evaluated. Utility is predicted success minus a fixed coefficient times predicted task cost. A separate subgroup uses models tagged open by the source metadata; that tag is not our license audit or evidence that the models run on a desktop. A label-and-cost-informed oracle is deliberately marked nondeployable. Its apparent performance is an upper bound conditional on these recorded attempts, never a usable router result.

8.3 Primary result: savings with an unacceptable quality loss

Policy Resolved Success Estimated inference USD/task USD/resolved task Saving vs GPT-5.2
GPT-5-mini alone 281/500 56.2% 0.0472 0.0840 90.0%
GPT-5.2 alone 364/500 72.8% 0.4736 0.6505 Reference
Expected random 50% mixture 322.5 expected 64.5% 0.2604 0.4037 45.0%
Primary learned 50% router 321/500 64.2% 0.2551 0.3974 46.1%

The primary router’s estimated inference total is US$127.5667, compared with US$236.7835 for the GPT-5.2 reference on the same 500 tasks. Its 46.1% saving comes with an 8.6 percentage-point resolution loss. The paired task-bootstrap 95% interval for the quality difference is approximately −11.6 to −5.6 points; the estimated saving interval is 40.8% to 51.4%. Repository-cluster sensitivity also fails the quality gate. The proposed three-point noninferiority margin is not supported. This is a negative result for the primary joint target, despite a substantial cost reduction.

The learned router also does not demonstrate a useful accuracy improvement over the expected random half-mixture: its paired difference is −0.3 points with a task-bootstrap 95% interval from −2.4 to +1.9 points. The corresponding cost ratio is 0.980, with interval 0.884 to 1.076. A cheaper policy is not useful evidence for the central hypothesis when its success falls outside the declared tolerance. The paired outcomes include 262 issues both models solve, 19 solved only by GPT-5-mini, 102 only by GPT-5.2, and 117 by neither. The existence of complementary successes does not imply that pre-task features can reliably identify them.

The primary router’s break-even additional overhead is about US$0.2184 per task; only US$0.1000 per task remains if a 25% inference-plus-overhead saving is the target. Adding a hypothetical US$0.05 overhead per task lowers its saving to 35.6%, without repairing the observed quality loss. These overhead values are sensitivity assumptions, not measured router or environment bills.

MiniMax-M2.5 alone resolves 379/500 at US$0.0733 per assigned task. Its historical estimated inference cost is 84.5% below the GPT-5.2 reference, with a three-point higher observed success rate. This is evidence about model choice in the archived comparison, not a routing effect and not a local-small- model result. Model size cannot be inferred from price or the word “mini”.

For illustration within the prespecified exploratory grid, the ten-model utility policy at coefficient 0.25 resolves 381/500 (76.2%) at US$0.1154 per task. Compared with GPT-5.2, that appears attractive: 75.6% lower estimated inference cost and 3.4 points more success. Compared with MiniMax alone, however, it adds only two resolved issues while costing approximately 57.4% more. These additional paired comparisons are explicitly labelled exploratory and conditional on the fitted policies. This operating point is not declared a winner after searching the grid. The whole grid and comparisons with the inexpensive standalone model are retained. Attributing all of the difference versus an expensive reference to intelligent routing would be misleading.

The recorded ten-model oracle resolves 87.8%, while the two-model oracle resolves 76.6%. These bounds suggest potential complementarity, but the oracles use the answers and realized costs. They do not demonstrate that an available router, personal agent or conversation policy can achieve those figures.

8.5 Statistical and economic limits

Intervals use 2,000 paired resamples and condition on the fitted cross-fold policies and the recorded outcomes; they do not refit the router inside every bootstrap sample. A repository-cluster sensitivity analysis uses only twelve clusters. Training and test folds can share repositories, so repository-unseen generalization is not established. One recorded attempt per model and task cannot estimate repeated-inference variance. Grid comparisons are exploratory and do not support a familywise claim from choosing their best point.

Upstream numerical costs are preserved rather than replaced by current prices. They are not independently audited invoices. Two unresolved Gemini entries report zero cost despite one API call each; these values are not proof of free inference. Neither the primary policy nor the illustrated portfolio selects those entries. Their effect on other policies is recorded in the supplementary cost-source checks. Router fitting took roughly two CPU seconds in this run, but no electricity, machine allocation or test-execution dollar rate was measured. Total operational cost and Codex subscription-credit savings remain unknown. No new model-inference purchase was needed for this replay.

The implications for the conversational study are concrete. First, retain a strong low-cost standalone model in the comparison. Second, ask whether runtime evidence and conversation improve the weak pre-task selection result. Third, measure all controller, expert, verification and failed-attempt usage before claiming savings. The replay supplies a reproducible benchmark finding and better controls; the causal bidirectional-conversation experiment still needs fresh metered execution.

9 Learning from verified interaction: prospective follow-up

This chapter specifies a follow-up to the fixed-model routing experiment. It does not report trained checkpoints, GPU measurements, distillation gains or RL results. First establish proprietary Luna/Sol prompt and routing performance; then replicate the small-only, large-only and cooperative comparisons with open-weight models. Learning is an additional intervention on that replication, not an explanation for the current proprietary results. Hosted Luna weights are not available to this project for fine-tuning.

9.1 Training data distinct from evaluation

Use executable repository tasks for training, rather than treating the final SWE-bench evaluation set as a source of demonstrations. Existing candidates are SWE-Gym, which supplies repository tasks with executable environments and test verification, and SWE-smith, which supplies generated repair tasks and released expert trajectories (Pan et al. 2025; Yang et al. 2025). Inspect pinned releases, licensing and provenance before acquisition. These are candidate sources; no training corpus from them has yet been assembled for this study. The existing LiveCodeBench solution-level training scaffold remains a separate, narrower algorithmic-code experiment, not repository-agent training.

Partition data before collecting adaptive trajectories. The training partition supports demonstrations, student rollouts, verifier feedback and weight updates. A separate development partition selects prompts, reward coefficients, checkpoints and stopping rules. A sealed evaluation panel measures the final learning curve after those decisions are locked. Tasks used to tune the current Pro prompts belong to development history and cannot later be called unseen evaluation. The already reserved validation tasks must likewise be retired from that role if their outcomes inform another update.

Prevent overlap by task identity, upstream issue/pull request, patch or near-copy similarity, and common synthetic ancestor. A mutation of a held-out task is not new training data. Group related issue families together. Where practical, reserve repositories for a separate cross-repository transfer evaluation; distinguish that endpoint from generalization to new issues in familiar repositories. Report language and repository composition, exclusions and pretraining-contamination limits. Benchmark train/test labels alone do not prove that two differently named releases are independent.

9.2 Observable traces and credit assignment

Record task and environment revisions, public instructions, visible assistant actions, tool inputs and observations, edits, public checks, failed approaches, delegation decisions, selected handoff context, expert messages and subsequent integration. Bind the final patch and external verification receipt to the trajectory, and record model identities, inference parameters, tokens, latency and cost evidence. Preserve unsuccessful episodes for analysis and controlled negative examples. Do not collect private model reasoning or place evaluator tests and reference patches in the policy context.

The current Codex journals retain structured controller/expert responses and tool-status hashes, but deliberately omit full tool inputs/outputs. They support routing analysis and selected public conversation examples; they are not a complete replayable action dataset. Future collection therefore needs a separately versioned observable-trace recorder. Do not retroactively invent missing actions or alter frozen trials to imply that complete traces existed.

Final success verifies the episode’s patch, not every intermediate action. Successful episodes can contain poor requests or incorrect expert suggestions. For supervised training, choose explicit targets: investigation/action sequences, help-request formulation, expert-answer integration, or verification. At a delegation decision the input ends before the expert’s future answer; hidden final grades cannot become features predicting when to ask. Mask tool and user tokens from the student loss. Expert messages are context unless the declared training target is a teacher demonstration of the student’s own role. Preserve state/action boundaries when chunking long trajectories.

9.3 Sequence and on-policy probability distillation

The sequence-distillation baseline trains a compatible student adapter on selected verified demonstrations using the maintained TRL/PEFT path. Text supervision does not require teacher/student tokenizer identity. Balance distinct tasks and disclose rejection rates, target-token exposure and selection bias; do not count many traces of one easy task as many independent tasks.

Following prior work on generative-model and on-policy distillation (Gu et al. 2024; Lu and Thinking Machines Lab 2025), the probability-distillation arm generates trajectories with the current student and obtains teacher probability feedback conditioned on those same visible histories. This tests correction in states reached by the student, rather than only imitation of expert-generated histories. Declare whether the objective uses full vocabulary distributions, truncated top-k distributions or a sampled-token estimator; these are different estimators, not interchangeable forms of complete logit access. Verify token-ID alignment, vocabulary, templates, temperature, masks and treatment of tool boundaries. Same-family model names do not establish compatibility.

Keep teacher and student identities, acquisition tasks and declared budgets matched across the sequence and probability arms. Changing teacher strength at the same time as the loss would confound the comparison.

Ordinary generation APIs can supply demonstrations. An on-policy scoring service must additionally score arbitrary supplied student sequences; log probabilities only for the teacher’s own sampled completion do not suffice. Self-hosted teacher weights or a suitable scoring API can provide that access. Full logits are not mandatory for every probability-distillation objective. Compare sample and compute efficiency empirically: richer supervision may reduce required examples while increasing teacher-scoring cost. Do not promise faster learning or software-task transfer from reasoning-benchmark evidence alone.

9.4 Reinforcement learning as a separate intervention

RL requires resettable training environments and fresh policy rollouts, not just a static conversation dataset. Use independently executed training-task correctness checks as the outcome signal, alongside explicit inference-cost accounting. Keep policy access separate from the verifier. Add terminal-state and test-integrity checks so editing checks, claiming tests passed, or declining all work cannot earn a successful-repair reward. Unavailable dependencies and infrastructure failures require a declared disposition, rather than an invented model-quality label.

Optimize cost subject to a quality constraint, or use a registered reward family and select its operating point on development data. Sweep cost coefficients on development only and report the resulting frontier; fewer expert calls alone are not success. Hold time, tool permissions and test access constant. Use a maintained agent-RL framework after validating its environment and action interfaces, rather than introducing an unverified custom optimizer.

Separate RL from base, sequence-SFT and probability-distillation conditions. If RL starts from an SFT checkpoint, the matched comparison is that exact SFT checkpoint with versus without RL, and the accumulated SFT cost remains in the RL condition. RL from the untouched base is a separate arm. Likewise, on-policy probability distillation is teacher-supervised learning; sharing rollout code with RL does not make the objectives equivalent.

9.5 Factorial controls and learning curves

Student checkpoint Small alone Small with frozen large expert
Untouched base Required Required
Sequence-distilled Required Required
Probability-distilled Required Required
Registered RL treatment Required Required

A fixed large-only model is the common capacity reference. Serve each eligible small checkpoint locally and remotely with identical weights/adapters and matched inference settings where supported. Document precision, quantization, runtime, context length and device differences; do not interpret a hosting or precision change as a training gain. Keep the expert revision and common task context fixed. Compare a frozen routing prompt with separately recalibrated routing only as explicitly separate controls. User memory and preferences are the same across arms and remain distinct from learned weights.

Start with a bounded integration pilot and freeze feasible data/compute milestones from its measured throughput before claiming a longitudinal study. Count distinct eligible task arrivals, verified demonstrations, target tokens, student rollouts and optimizer updates separately. Register acquisition order, seeds and checkpoint selection before evaluation. Compare incremental updates with restarting from the same base on accumulated data when budget permits; do not assume that more rounds cause monotonic improvement. Measure forgetting and transfer on tasks outside the adapted workload.

Plot resolution against total inference cost at each registered checkpoint, separately for independent and cooperative operation. Plot learning against distinct tasks, teacher tokens, GPU-hours, elapsed time and measured expenditure. Include a lifecycle view: acquisition plus scoring plus training cost, amortized over a stated number of later tasks, together with their inference cost. Report the break-even workload only when measured training expense and positive per-task saving support it; otherwise it is unknown or absent. Distinguish published token-rate scenarios from observed charges and local hardware costs.

All arms face the same frozen evaluation tasks and budgets. Report paired successes and failures, expert-assisted task fraction, consultation count, verification failures, latency and uncertainty. Evaluate frozen checkpoints on the sealed panel only after training and analysis choices are locked; use fresh development panels for adaptive monitoring. The target remains at least 95% relative large-only accuracy with at least 95% lower total task inference cost. Training may shift the frontier without reaching that target; lifecycle savings require additional evidence. No current result establishes either learning or amortized-cost improvement.

10 Discussion and limits

The literature makes the central hypothesis plausible without making it new or settled. EdgeWise reports substantial cloud-API savings with small changes in software-task performance under particular conditions, but its accounting excludes the local SLM. Router-R1 and related work already make the router an active participant that reasons across model responses. The present study must therefore establish its value through reproducible comparisons, complete cost measurement and a precise intervention, rather than the assertion that models have never conversed before.

The proposed distinction is continuing expert dialogue: an expert can ask for missing evidence, challenge an interpretation and revise a proposal while the small controller continues working. That may prevent context omissions and uncritical acceptance. It may also waste time, encourage circular conversation or amplify a shared mistake. Compare it directly with one-way assistance and reset expert sessions under equal budgets. A bidirectional API alone is not a scientific contribution; the empirical finding, including a negative result, is the contribution.

The complete SWE-bench Verified replay sharpens this requirement. The primary pre-task router saves estimated inference dollars but loses too much quality, and a strong inexpensive standalone model undercuts the apparent advantage of several portfolio operating points. A conversational agent must therefore beat credible cheap standalone alternatives, not merely reduce calls to a costly reference. The replay is a standard-benchmark result, while its historical single-attempt data and unmeasured deployment expenses restrict its claims.

The pilot’s lack of optional consultations is a useful design lesson. Easy tasks can show that a controller avoids unnecessary expert work, but cannot evaluate its capacity to obtain help. The next development sample should span observed difficulty and failure modes before the final test is frozen. It must not select final tasks merely because they make conversation look useful. A registered development-stratified sampling rule, followed by an untouched test sample, can ensure both easy and difficult assignments without selecting on final-treatment outcomes.

The artifact-policy problem also matters. In a product, adding a good test to an existing file is usually desirable. In a controlled repair benchmark, altering the tests used for evaluation can invalidate success. The next protocol should make that distinction explicit: immutable evaluator tests are outside the worker, while permitted public-test additions are reviewed or applied under a declared patch policy. The current frozen results remain intact. Reinterpreting them as proof that conversational agents cannot follow constraints would be unwarranted given the prompt ambiguity and tiny sample.

Personalization and long-term learning remain optional, separable questions. Editable memory has practical value as a user interface, but it does not automatically improve task success. Existing developer-skill research motivates generic and shuffled-user controls. RL can improve decisions without providing an economical training path at small scale. Training cost, privacy boundaries, feedback reliability and retained local capability must be measured. The current code uses no model-weight update, and the live Codex experiment has no access to the hosted models’ weights.

More agents can supply complementary expertise, but also introduce duplicate work and harder credit assignment. The minimal dyadic design should establish when conversation helps before a many-to-many experiment claims emergent roles or self-improvement. Existing graph and multi-agent learning frameworks should be reused for that extension. The long-term ambition remains affordable, user-controlled AI; that social objective is not demonstrated by a four-task hosted-model pilot.

11 Reproducibility and next execution

The repository contains the full protocol and adapted benchmark provenance, separate task workspaces, immutable grader source, regression reports, submitted patches, nullable-cost records, dialogue transcript and analysis code. It also contains a tested restore command that verifies downloaded archive hashes and replays all buggy/fixed controls before creating new worker copies. It refuses to overwrite existing destinations. The original source and evaluator trees are checked against their manifest before grading.

From a prepared research environment, the recorded analysis can be reproduced without any model calls:

python scripts/analyze_codex_pilot.py --output-dir results/my-pilot-analysis
python -m pytest -q

On a fresh compatible workspace, restore the historical benchmark fixtures:

python scripts/restore_codex_pilot.py --install-env
python scripts/restore_codex_pilot.py --verify-only

The analysis command requires the research dependencies in requirements-research.lock. Restore uses its separately pinned CPython 3.8.20 environment and legacy test dependencies, and downloads the exact registered public archives. The study is deliberately an adapted BugsInPy subset; the restore process does not claim to recreate every original benchmark environment. Do not execute new models in the recorded solved worker copies.

For a normal machine with a writable, authenticated Codex installation, the reusable adapter accepts a task manifest and a new output directory:

python -m ttgl.personal --task task.json --condition personal \
  --small-model gpt-6-luna --large-model gpt-6.1-sol \
  --max-expert-calls 2 --timeout-seconds 240 \
  --output-dir artifacts/new-conversation

The runbook documents the exact supported arguments, structured responses, resumed threads, failure disposition and grading boundary. Completion means the controller finished; it does not automatically mean the issue was resolved. A fake backend verifies control flow; real native trials separately verify runtime availability and per-model token metering. Earlier managed-host read-only failures remain archived historical evidence. They are not the state of the writable desktop continuation, which completed all 141 fresh assignments across the original, development and held-out panels. The earlier BugsInPy pilot used the collaboration tool; those records remain distinct from native trials.

The six-condition SWE-bench bridge implements mandatory native model/metering preflight, isolated source checkouts, official prediction export and grade import. scripts/collect_codex_usage.py uses the supported per-thread estimate route without new inference. Native completion counters are cumulative, so the independent audit checks response identity and validated counter deltas before reconciling total and per-model usage. Missing bills remain unknown.

Reproduce the completed held-out audit and target analysis without new models:

PYTHONPATH=src python scripts/audit_live_study.py \
  --study-dir results/delegation-heldout-001/study-002 \
  --output artifacts/my-heldout-audit.json
ttgl_analysis=results/delegation-heldout-001/analysis-002
python scripts/report_policy_target.py \
  --records "$ttgl_analysis/published-rate-records.json" \
  --output artifacts/my-heldout-target.json

Use fresh output paths; these commands must not replace archived evidence. The handover records source freezes, actual process state and gates for continuing the bounded Pro comparison. A passing software check or environment fixture is not a task success. The Pro control, real actor boundary and pristine patch replay must pass before scored model trials. No new GPU or provider purchase is authorized as a workaround. Open-weight training remains a later protocol, and its costs must be measured separately.

12 Conclusion

Small-model-led collaboration is established prior art, including learned delegation for software engineering. The defensible hypothesis is whether continuing, bounded conversation achieves materially lower total cost while retaining a prespecified level of task success, beyond single-model execution, initial routing and one-way assistance. Personal memory and learned skills can be tested as additional interventions.

The present work implements and tests the orchestration and measurement code, executes a historical-bug pilot and 141 fresh metered assignments, and replays all 500 SWE-bench Verified tasks across ten published model runs. The primary historical router saves 46.1% in estimated inference cost but loses 8.6 quality points. Cheap strong standalone controls explain why model selection alone is not evidence for a routing advantage.

The completed eleven-task held-out conversational comparison improves the observed Luna resolution count from seven to eight while Sol resolves nine. It saves 91.45% of the Sol model-inference scenario cost and retains 88.89% of Sol accuracy, missing both 95/95 components. One voluntary bidirectional rescue is accompanied by imperfect context transfer, unsuccessful consultation on another task, and an unresolved missed escalation. These results show useful mechanism behavior and a limited descriptive improvement, not reliable failure detection, a causal expert effect or population noninferiority. The prospective Pro comparison retains standalone controls and pre-consultation candidate patches to test those remaining questions before any learning claims.
